clinicalPearls: Results from aspiration or inhalation of lipid-containing material, most classically mineral oil, laxatives, oil-based nasal drops, lip balms and, increasingly, vaping oils.
Predisposing factors include impaired swallowing, gastro-oesophageal reflux, neurological disease, structural upper airway abnormalities and habitual use of oily preparations at bedtime.
Presentation ranges from an incidental radiographic finding to chronic cough, dyspnoea and low-grade fever; acute massive aspiration can cause severe pneumonitis.
Imaging characteristically shows consolidation or masses with low (fat) attenuation on computed tomography, a highly suggestive finding when present.
A crazy-paving pattern on high-resolution computed tomography can occur and overlaps with several other interstitial processes.
Bronchoalveolar lavage demonstrating abundant lipid-laden macrophages supports the diagnosis, and fat stains on cytology or biopsy are confirmatory.
Cessation of exposure is the cornerstone of management; the offending lipid source must be identified and removed.
It can mimic malignancy radiologically, sometimes prompting biopsy to exclude a lung tumour.
reference.pathophysiology: Exogenous lipoid pneumonia arises when lipid material enters the lower respiratory tract, usually by aspiration in individuals with impaired airway protection or by chronic low-volume inhalation of oily substances. Mineral and other mineral-derived oils are poorly cleared because they are chemically inert and do not stimulate the cough reflex effectively, allowing them to reach the alveoli. There the oil is emulsified and engulfed by alveolar macrophages, which become distended and lipid-laden; as these cells die they release the lipid back into the interstitium and alveolar spaces, perpetuating a chronic foreign-body-type inflammatory reaction. Over time this leads to a granulomatous and fibrotic response with infiltration by lymphocytes and giant cells, disruption of alveolar architecture and, in longstanding cases, interstitial fibrosis. Vegetable and animal fats may provoke a more pronounced acute inflammatory reaction because they can be hydrolysed by lung lipases into irritant free fatty acids, whereas inert mineral oils tend to produce a more indolent, chronic picture with characteristic fat-density lesions.
additionalDifferentials: Bronchogenic carcinoma or other lung neoplasm
Endogenous lipoid pneumonia from distal airway obstruction
additionalInvestigations: High-resolution computed tomography of the thorax assessing for low-attenuation (fat-density) consolidation
Bronchoscopy with bronchoalveolar lavage for lipid-laden macrophages
Special fat stains on lavage fluid or tissue such as oil red O or Sudan stains
Transbronchial or surgical lung biopsy when malignancy cannot be excluded
Detailed exposure history including medicines, nasal drops, cosmetics and inhalant or vaping use
Swallowing assessment and evaluation for gastro-oesophageal reflux where aspiration is suspected
Microbiological studies to exclude concurrent infection
redFlags: A mass-like lesion that cannot be confidently distinguished from carcinoma
Acute large-volume aspiration with rapidly progressive respiratory failure
Progressive dyspnoea and hypoxaemia indicating extensive parenchymal involvement
Radiological or clinical progression despite removal of the lipid source
reference.prognosis: Outcome is generally good when the causative exposure is identified and stopped early, with gradual radiological and symptomatic improvement in many cases; chronic unrecognised exposure may lead to persistent consolidation, fibrosis or complications from acute severe aspiration.
pitfalls: Missing the diagnosis by not taking a specific history of oil-based medications, nasal drops or vaping.
Misinterpreting a fat-density mass as malignancy and pursuing aggressive intervention unnecessarily.
Attributing chronic consolidation solely to infection and giving repeated antibiotic courses.
Failing to recognise ongoing aspiration risk, allowing continued exposure and disease progression.
Overlooking the entity in older or neurologically impaired patients using bedtime oily laxatives.
references: Fishman's Pulmonary Diseases and Disorders (standard reference)
